Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old patient with a several-day history of dry cough and nasal congestion, likely a viral upper respiratory infection; symptomatic care advised with follow-up if not improving.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Dry, persistent cough for about 5–6 days; runny nose; nighttime coughing; throat irritation from coughing.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began ~5–6 days ago; persistent; fatigue; chills; possible feverish sensation (shivering).
- Associated symptoms: Fatigue/weakness; sore throat from coughing; no chest pain; no dyspnea; no ear symptoms; no nausea/vomiting; diarrhea early in illness but resolved; appetite overall OK.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension.
- Medications: Metformin; Lisinopril.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Social history: Lives with partner; former smoker (quit 6 months ago); alcohol: wine, about 2–3 glasses on 2–3 evenings per week; occupation: IT developer; generally well otherwise.
- Family history: Father with type 2 diabetes.
- Preventive care: Not otherwise detailed.

Examination:
- (No formal vitals or physical examination findings documented.)

Impression:
- Acute viral upper respiratory infection (likely viral illness) with dry cough and fatigue; no evidence of bacterial pneumonia at this time.

Plan:
- Symptoms management: rest; maintain hydration; regular paracetamol as needed (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Follow-up: return in 2–3 days if not improving; return sooner if fever develops or cough/wellness worsens; consider re-evaluation if symptoms persist beyond ~4 days.
- Antibiotics: may consider antibiotics for chest infection if feverish and cough persists/worsens (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Work: limit exposure; take a day or two off if possible; return to work early next week if improving.
- Safety net: seek care sooner if breathing worsens or new concerning symptoms arise.
- Lifestyle counsel: reduce alcohol intake due to diabetes/hypertension; suggested target: two glasses per week initially, then further reduction if feasible; no direct changes to current diabetes/hypertension medications (continue Metformin and Lisinopril).

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: vital signs and any exam findings not documented; vaccination status not recorded; no explicit meds reconciliation beyond current meds; no imaging or lab results ordered.
- Internal conflicts: None detected.
- Transcript quality: Generally coherent; some interruptions/noise and repetitive questioning, but actionable details present.
